item.title: Ukraine pushes back on Trump's call for a new president as drones hit Russian data hub
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
WASHINGTON (AP) — U.S. President Donald Trump on Sunday said Russia and Ukraine have agreed to an “energy ceasefire” without offering specifics on terms. Neither side immediately commented on such an agreement. The announcement comes a day after Trump blamed Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy for attacking diesel facilities in Russia and contributing to a global shortage. Russia and Ukraine have repeatedly attacked each other’s energy infrastructure during the war. Trump’s brief post said only that the ceasefire takes effect immediately and that both sides had agreed to it. “Do not break it!” he said in his social media post. The White House did not immediately clarify the president’s post or add detail. THIS IS A BREAKING NEWS UPDATE. Check back for updates. AP’s earlier story follows below. Only Russia is responsible for the war in Ukraine, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Sunday as he vowed to press ahead with strikes on Russian oil refineries , despite criticism from U.S. President Donald Trump, who blamed him for high diesel prices and said he should be replaced. The exchange came as Kyiv pressed its campaign against infrastructure deep inside Russia, with a drone attack on Sunday shutting down a data center run by Russian technology giant Yandex, the third strike on the company’s facilities in four days. Russia and Ukraine are locked in a long-range aerial war while their armies remain largely deadlocked on the front line, more than 4 1/2 years since Moscow’s full-scale invasion . “Ukraine will be ready to stop striking Russian oil refineries if Russia stops striking our energy infrastructure,” Zelenskyy wrote on X. “It is possible to stop strikes on energy infrastructure as early as today, but (Russian President Vladimir) Putin does not want to do so,” he said, adding that any de-escalation must be reciprocal and backed by real guarantees. Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha pushed back on Trump's comments, writing on X late Saturday that Zelenskyy was leading the country through a war for its independence. “He has the support of the Ukrainian people, and they have the right to decide. Statements from abroad only confirm that he is doing his job well,” Sybiha wrote. Trump said Saturday it was time for Ukraine to get a new president , suggesting Zelenskyy has not done enough to end the war and blaming him for high diesel prices in the U.S. “I suggest they get a new leader who can make a deal because he could have made many deals and for some reason he never does,” Trump said. The U.S. president, who on Friday struck a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to buy diesel from Russia in an attempt to address high fuel prices ahead of the U.S. midterm elections, has been urging Zelenskyy for weeks to stop strikes on Russian energy infrastructure. He has sought to blame record U.S. diesel prices on Ukraine rather than the U.S.-led war in Iran, which has driven up world energy prices. Ukrainian and European officials reacted to the diesel deal with dismay, saying it will help pay for Russia’s war effort. Ukraine strikes third data center in four days The Ukrainian drone attack on the Yandex data center in the city of Vladimir, east of Moscow, caused outages across the company's services, leaving users in dozens of Russian cities and in Kazakhstan, Belarus and Armenia unable to order taxis or access banking services, according to Russian independent news outlet Astra. “As a result of the drone attack, the infrastructure of Yandex’s data center in Vladimir was damaged. Operations at the data center have been completely halted. There were no injuries,” said the Yandex Cloud Telegram channel, which provides operational updates on service availability. In Moscow, residents described disruption to everyday tasks. Pavel Belyavskiy, a driver for Yandex Taxi, said it was unclear whether orders were coming through at all, and that on several rides he had to cancel after waiting a long time because he could not reach the passenger. “I’d press the ‘call’ button to contact them, but nothing happens,” he said, “There’s nothing I can do, so I’m just forced to cancel.” Igor Mann said he went to check the status of an order on the Yandex Market shopping platform but the page was unavailable, and connecting through a VPN did not help. “Nothing worked,” he said. Another Moscow resident, Eduard Malyavko, said the outages had “direct impact” and weren't just about “convenience.” “It’s also about work,” he said, adding that they also affected “healthcare, and everything else.” On Thursday, a drone attack took a Yandex data center offline in the Ryazan region, southeast of Moscow. A day later, Ukrainian drones hit the company’s major data center in the Kaluga region, southwest of Moscow, partly putting it out of action, Yandex said. Yandex, often described as Russia’s Google, runs the country’s most popular search engine and a wide range of digital services, and is heavily involved in Russia’s artificial intelligence development. Zaporizhzhia death toll rises to 23 Elsewhere, Zelenskyy said search and rescue operations ended in the southern city of Zaporizhzhia after a Russian bombing on Saturday, Ivan Fedorov, the former regional head and co-chair of the regional defense council, said Sunday. Zelenskyy said 23 people were killed in the attack, including four children. More than 30 people were wounded, Fedorov said, eight of whom remain hospitalized. A man was killed and two women wounded in a Ukrainian drone strike on Russia's Bryansk border region, local officials said Sunday. ___ Morton reported from London. item.title: American citizen among at least 12 people killed in blast at Saudi Arabia airport
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia on September 19, 2026. - AFP/Getty Images At least 12 people were killed and hundreds wounded when Yemen’s Houthi militants struck Riyadh’s international airport with a missile on Saturday, in Saudi Arabia’s deadliest attack in more than a decade. It was the third missile strike this week on the King Khalid International Airport, which has been closed until at least late Sunday, leading to the cancellation of more than 600 flights. The missile struck a terminal building, killing four Saudis, two Bangladeshis, an American, an Egyptian, a Jordanian, a Syrian, a Palestinian, and a Sudanese, the kingdom’s civil aviation body said Sunday, adding that 309 people were wounded. Following the attack, US President Donald Trump said he was considering joining Saudi strikes against the Houthis in Yemen, having previously resisted Saudi requests for direct military intervention. One traveler told Reuters news agency they saw something fly across the sky outside the airport before part of the ceiling near a departure gate collapsed. Another recalled hearing an explosion before seeing several people lying wounded on the ground. An eyewitness video released by Reuters showed large boards and debris strewn across the terminal floor, with people moving through a dust-filled hall. King Khalid International Airport, Saudi Arabia’s second-busiest, serves the capital, Riyadh, a city of about eight million people. Nasr al-Din Amer, a senior Houthi official, appeared to acknowledge responsibility, writing on X: “We shut down Riyadh international airport.” The US, UK, Spain and Canada are among countries warning their citizens against using the airport. Saturday’s incident has exposed vulnerabilities in the kingdom’s defense capabilities as it wages an air campaign in support of Yemen’s internationally recognized government, which is fighting the Houthis on the ground. With Iranian assistance, the Houthis have built up a large arsenal of missiles, including ballistic weapons, as well as a range of drones. A Houthi military statement Sunday reiterated a warning to all airlines and travelers against using Saudi airports and airspace, “as they are vulnerable to targeting… with the exception of Mecca and Medina airports.” “Saudi Arabia will bear responsibility for any failed attempts to intercept” missiles, the Houthi statement said, and it would continue responding to “blockades with blockades, and escalation with escalation.” The group has also warned airliners against using Saudi airspace. ‘We’ll make a decision’ Trump said Saturday he plans to speak with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman following the attack. “They’re able to defend. The Saudis are good fighters. But I think the attack was a terrible thing,” Trump said when asked whether Saudi Arabia could defend itself against the Houthis. People gather outside a metro station on the road to King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, on October 10, 2026. - AP People gather outside a metro station on the road to King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, on October 10, 2026. - AP Asked outside the White House whether Washington planned to join Saudi strikes on the Houthis, a militia aligned with US foe Iran, Trump told reporters: “We may. We’re going to look at it.” “We just found out about the recent attack, so we’ll make a decision. We move very quickly.” Last month, Trump rejected two appeals from Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman for US strikes against the Houthis, CNN reported at the time. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio confirmed a US citizen was among those killed and condemned the attacks as showing “a blatant disregard for innocent civilian life,” in a post on X. Wounded people, including some in critical condition, were rushed to hospitals Saturday by ambulance and helicopter, people familiar with the matter told Reuters. Two previous attacks at the airport this week killed four people and caused heavy damage to a Saudi commercial plane. UN Special Envoy for Yemen Hans Grundberg called the attacks “a grave escalation” that poses a serious threat to regional security, in a post on X. unknown content item - United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres condemned the latest strike and said “attacks on civilians and civilian infrastructure are a violation of international law,” also writing on X. Saudi miscalculations The civil war in Yemen flared up once again this summer and significantly intensified last month, after years of relative calm. In retaliation for a Saudi blockade on the Yemeni capital Sanaa, the Houthis announced in July they would target Saudi shipping in the Red Sea, and began a campaign of missile attacks against Saudi infrastructure, including oil refineries. Last month, they conducted a lightning offensive along Yemen’s Red Sea coast, capturing the port of Mocha and closing in on Taiz, Yemen’s third-largest city. That led the Saudi-backed Yemeni government based in Aden to launch a major offensive, but it has struggled to retake much ground. Saudi Arabia has for 11 years tried to contain the conflict on its southern border through military force and diplomacy – first waging war with the Houthis, then pursuing peace talks with them and restoring diplomatic talks with their backer, Tehran. Despite the efforts, a series of miscalculations has left Riyadh exposed to further conflict in Yemen, experts say. Saudi Arabia ended its longstanding partnership with the UAE late last year over its backing of a rival force in Yemen, misjudged Trump’s willingness to back it if it needed support, and struggled to organize disintegrated armed factions fighting the Houthis. The escalation threatens Saudi Arabia’s broader ambitions to become an international destination for business and tourism. On Sunday, the Saudi energy ministry said the World Petroleum Congress began as scheduled in Riyadh, but it’s unclear how many delegates are attending. CNN’s Ibrahim Dahman, Michael Williams and Mostafa Salem contributed reporting. item.title: Republicans want Abdul El-Sayed to be the main character of the midterms. He's on board.
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
PORT HURON, Mich. (AP) — Abdul El-Sayed , holding a handheld mic and wearing his signature V-neck black shirt, slowly shook his head as a woman at his town hall described how she burned through her savings after undergoing emergency brain surgery. “I’m really sorry for your experience, and I hope that you’re on the mend,” said El-Sayed, the Democratic candidate for U.S. Senate in Michigan, after outlining proposals for guaranteed health care and paid leave. Later that night, while talking to reporters in the basement below the theatre, his tone was far different. El-Sayed called his Republican opponent Mike Rogers a “coward,” said President Donald Trump was “afraid” to visit the state and dismissed as “dumb” a question about whether Iran or Israel posed a greater threat to the United States. The exchanges captured two sides of a candidate who is the central figure in one of the nation’s most consequential Senate races . El-Sayed would be the country's first Muslim senator, and he's crisscrossing the state to counter a Republican effort, fueled by tens of millions of dollars, to portray him as a dangerous radical. But he has also embraced his confrontational side by mocking and taunting Trump and Rogers. “If they want to make me the main character in the midterms, I’m not shying away from it,” El-Sayed said in an interview. “Run against me. See how well that works out for you.” El-Sayed’s brash, swaggering confidence rubbed some Democrats the wrong way during a divisive primary against Rep. Haley Stevens. The former public health official has shown little interest in toning it down, remaining unapologetic about his progressive agenda and adversarial approach, emboldening supporters who believe he's the right candidate for an angry electorate that has lost faith in the political establishment. But his doubters fear he'll cost Democrats control of the Senate by failing to unite his party's disparate factions ahead of November. “If you want their votes, you have to make nice with those people, and he’s not really doing that,” said Michigan political strategist Adrian Hemond, who supported Stevens. “Maybe he doesn’t have to. The entire theory of this candidacy has been he can remake what the electorate looks like.” Republicans target El-Sayed Even though Michigan backed Trump twice in his three presidential campaigns, no Republican has won a Senate race in the state since 1994. The political landscape is no friendlier this year . Trump started an unpopular war with Iran, leading to higher gas prices. Rogers has opted for a low-key campaign with fewer public events than El-Sayed as he tries to make the race all about his Democratic opponent. As of Oct. 10, Republicans had outspent Democrats by $78 million to $63 million in the Michigan Senate race, according to AdImpact, which tracks political advertising. Around $40 million in Republican spending has gone toward negative advertisements, compared to only around $20 million from Democrats. The ads portray El-Sayed as “dangerously radical” and “too extreme,” highlighting his past calls to defund the police and relax immigration enforcement. Others tie him to Hasan Piker, a popular online streamer with whom El-Sayed has appeared and who has drawn criticism for past comments, including saying that “America deserved 9/11.” On Friday, Rogers appeared alongside Louisiana Sen. John Kennedy, who told reporters that El-Sayed “sleeps in a Bin Laden jersey.” Rogers laughed. Vice President JD Vance has called him “evil.” In one social media post, Trump shared a photo of himself with first lady Melania Trump alongside a photo of El-Sayed and his wife, who wears a hijab, with the caption: “Two VERY DIFFERENT America’s.” Late Wednesday, Trump referred to El-Sayed as “Mohammed” and said he “goes back to the days of the Jihad.” El-Sayed has hardly backed down. At the campaign stop in Port Huron, he taunted Trump to visit Michigan, suggesting Rogers and other Republicans were afraid the president would hurt their chances. “Donald, if you’re watching, don’t wuss out, man,” El-Sayed said. And he responded to Kennedy’s attack by suggesting the Republican is in the KKK. “That’s rich coming from someone who wears his bed sheets out at night,” El-Sayed posted on social media. El-Sayed uses a personal touch with voters Before the Port Huron town hall, El-Sayed worked his way down a line of people who couldn’t fit inside the theater, shaking hands, taking photos and stopping for conversations. Jeff Petrucella and his wife Alice traveled from Macomb County to see El-Sayed. They described themselves as politically “middle of the road” and said they had voted Republican in the past. “I’m pretty done with the Republicans right now,” Jeff said. Alice said she was “looking for a change that is better for my granddaughters,” pointing to El-Sayed’s support for Medicare for All. Nor was she put off by his more confrontational appearances on Fox News. “I think he expresses himself well. You can tell he’s a well-spoken, educated man,” she said. Pat Kreiner was among those who waited nearly an hour to see El-Sayed. Her children had persuaded her to support him in the Democratic primary. “My son said to me, ‘I have been living with this trickle-down economy since the day I was born,’” Kreiner said. “‘It doesn’t work for me.’” Kreiner also expressed anger about Trump's trade war with Canada, just across the river from Port Huron. “We are heartsick about our neighbors,” she said. “They used to come over a lot. We don’t see them now.” Visiting smaller towns such as Port Huron has become central to El-Sayed’s campaign, with his team recently saying he's held more than 500 events in over 100 cities across the state. “Go everywhere. Talk to everyone. That’s what we do,” El-Sayed said in an interview. The personal approach has not erased all the skepticism surrounding El-Sayed, including within his own party. His criticism of Israel and association with Piker have raised concerns among some Jewish Democrats. El-Sayed has held a series of private gatherings with undecided Jewish voters as he works to win their support. He has also sought to strengthen his standing with Black voters. In the Democratic primary, Stevens drew more support in Wayne County, home to Detroit and its large Black population. Ahead of Thursday’s debate, El-Sayed attended two events with Black leaders before stopping at a Black barbershop, where he moved from chair to chair talking with customers. He stopped at one point to speak with a pregnant woman, congratulating her and asking when her baby was due. “November 8th?” El-Sayed joked. “Make sure you vote early, huh?” The race has become about more than just Michigan While El-Sayed has spent much of his campaign trying to win over Michigan voters, his candidacy has taken on significance far beyond the state. Republicans have made him a symbol of what they warn is an increasingly radical Democratic Party, while progressives see his campaign as a chance to prove their politics can win in a closely divided state. At a New York City fundraiser on Oct. 5, Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez cast his campaign as a test for progressives nationwide. “If Abdul can win in Michigan, anybody can win anywhere,” said the New York Democrat, a potential presidential candidate. Ocasio-Cortez plans to campaign with El-Sayed in Michigan next week, followed by former President Barack Obama on Oct. 24 . The national stakes have also drawn renewed opposition. United Democracy Project, a super PAC affiliated with AIPAC, disclosed an initial $94,000 expenditure against El-Sayed on Friday, after spending nearly $30 million to oppose him in the Democratic primary. And El-Sayed, despite insisting the election should focus on Michigan voters and their economic struggles, has embraced the larger implications of his candidacy. “I am grateful for your support,” he told the audience at the New York fundraiser, according to remarks obtained by The Associated Press. He said he had two goals — “pick up a U.S. Senate seat” and “change the nature of our politics for the better.” This article originally appeared on Associated Press at https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/republicans-want-abdul-el-sayed-112552011.html

item.title: Wall Street banks had a blockbuster first half. Higher rates could change everything.
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Wall Street's biggest banks entered the second half of 2026 after one of their most profitable six-month runs in at least a decade. Then interest rates surged. When they kick off third quarter earnings on Tuesday, starting with JPMorgan Chase ( JPM ), Goldman Sachs ( GS ), and Citigroup ( C ), followed by Bank of America ( BAC ) and Morgan Stanley ( MS ) on Wednesday, investors will be hunting for clues around whether sharply rising interest rates are beginning to spoil the first-half boom. Profits at these giants should fall from last quarter, as their revenues from trading, dealmaking, and financing are expected to retreat from the levels that powered standout second quarter results, according to analyst estimates compiled by Bloomberg. Still, most are expected to show profits rose from a year ago, with Bank of America and Morgan Stanley expected to prove the exceptions. "Right now, you look out the window, and it feels okay. I think this is more about the risks than what's happening out the window," said Brendan Coughlin, president of regional lender Citizens Financial Group ( CFG ), which reports later next week. The mood among investors has already soured. Collectively, these five banks have shed about $270 billion in market value from their respective summer highs through Friday's close, even as the S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ) remains up roughly 14% this year. "A great deal of the recent underperformance for banks has been driven by the dramatic rise in long-term rates," UBS analyst Erika Najarian recently told clients. A Truist Securities survey earlier this month found just 35% of institutional investors expect bank stocks to outperform the broader market, down from 68% in July and 82% in December. The key focus for investors next week is less on what higher borrowing costs mean for third quarter profits than on whether the rapid repricing of money will begin to undermine the unusually strong activity that defined 2026's first half. Higher rates can initially lift banks' lending income, but they also raise deposit and wholesale funding costs, pressure bond portfolios, and complicate math for dealmakers. The speed of the move in rates also adds unease. Macquarie strategists noted this week that many of the highest-profile financial blowups over the past 50 years happened shortly after abrupt moves in long-term bond yields. Trading results are expected to bring the most immediate evidence for a Wall Street slowdown. In September, bank executives telegraphed softer activity , particularly in fixed income, compared to the frenzy that kicked up this spring. JPMorgan is among the big Wall Street banks reporting earnings this coming week. (Reuters/Eduardo Munoz/File Photo) Reuters / REUTERS Higher financing costs also raise the stakes for whether momentum in this year's investment banking surge can continue into 2027. Several companies, including smart ring maker Oura, have postponed plans to go public, citing market conditions. In a sign that even AI-related firms faced a higher capital hurdle, Nvidia-backed Firmus Grid abruptly shelved public listing plans this week after investors balked at its proposed valuation. Global merger and acquisitions deal announcements also slowed sharply during the third quarter . But the caution hasn't eliminated the opportunity Wall Street sees financing the AI build-out, which could churn out years of debt, equity and advisory work for banks. "Yes, the interest rate environment is not helpful, but as a topic in the boardroom, M&A hasn't slowed down," Guillermo Baygual, Citigroup's global co-head of M&A, told Yahoo Finance earlier this week. A separate focus across all banks is whether executives indicate that deposit and other funding costs will pressure lending margins. The Federal Reserve raised its benchmark policy rate last month amid already fierce competition among US lenders to bring in more customer cash. "Loan growth is easier to find than deposit growth, and so it's putting pressure on deposit dynamics of raising funds," Citizens' Coughlin said. David Hollerith covers a range of developments throughout the financial sector, from Wall Street to banking and asset management to crypto and fintech. Email him at david.hollerith@yahoofinance.com. Follow him on X at @DsHollers. item.title: Next steps in the Cornell sexual assault case — and the challenges that lie ahead
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
New York Gov. Kathy Hochul has tapped Attorney General Letitia James (right) to be the special prosecutor in the Cornell University sexual assault case. They attended a press conference on October 2 in New York. - NDZ/STAR MAX/IPx/AP When New York Gov. Kathy Hochul appointed Attorney General Letitia James to take over the investigation into an alleged gang rape at a fraternity house at Cornell University, she asked for a “fresh and thorough” review of all the evidence. And there is a lot of evidence. Far from the two-party “he said-she said” structure of many sexual assault allegations, the Cornell case features seven men accused of wrongdoing in a civil suit filed by the woman known as Jane Doe. There are interviews with Doe, the accused men and other witnesses ; scores of texts and Snapchat posts ; secretly recorded phone calls ; and lengthy, conflicting reports from the police, district attorney and university investigators about who knew what when. In all, it’s a far cry from the limited evidence the local prosecutor said he reviewed before deciding not to bring charges in 2024. Putting the array of evidence together represents the primary task ahead for James, the special prosecutor tasked with leading the investigation and considering whether to bring charges. How the investigation proceeds will be closely watched by community members, university students and advocacy groups across the country. “There is literally an avalanche of statements to collect in this case that apparently were not reviewed by the original prosecutor,” said Paul DerOhannesian, an Albany-based attorney and author of “Sexual Assault Trials.” “Getting all those statements is a big task,” he said. Mimi Rocah, former Westchester County district attorney and former federal prosecutor, likened the work ahead to “putting the pieces of the puzzle together.” Hochul laid out the questions James will try to answer in a news conference on October 2. “Attorney General James will be the one who puts a spotlight on this case and says, ‘Who knew what when?’ ‘What did they do wrong?’ ‘Why didn’t they come forward?’ and ‘How was this woman denied justice?’ and we anticipate that will come out over the right period of time,” Hochul said. For James, the investigation faces several key challenges ahead, including the potential loss of evidence two years after the fact, questions about her potential bias, a supposed “loophole” in New York’s sexual assault law and intense pressure from the community. The most important job of a special prosecutor, Rocah said, is “to try to conduct a fair process and really convey that to the public and be transparent at the end of the day about what you did and why you did it.” The immediate next steps for James At the news conference, James laid out her next steps as special prosecutor. “Every New Yorker deserves to know that when they report a crime, it will be investigated fully and fairly. That they will be seen and heard,” she said. “We will review the facts, gather evidence, interview witnesses and, if warranted, pursue prosecutions.” unknown content item - Much of the evidence may already exist. Notably, Cornell held its own formal Title IX investigation, the federal civil rights law banning discrimination based on gender – which includes sexual harassment and violence. The investigation included more than 50 interviews, including with all of the men accused of wrongdoing, except one who declined to be interviewed, according to a heavily redacted 99-page document summarizing the panel’s findings. CNN has not seen the Title IX filings, which are generally confidential and restricted to the parties involved. Separately, Cornell is reviewing its own response to the sexual assault allegations. This review, led by former US Deputy Attorney General Sally Q. Yates, will examine how Cornell “prevents and responds to sexual harassment, sexual assault and related misconduct on campus,” the university said . Cornell University campus in Ithaca, New York. - Surya Vaidy/CNN Still, James will have the opportunity to reinterview certain witnesses rather than simply relying on previous evidence. DerOhannesian said James will have a few extra tools at her disposal in this investigation. She could try to cut a deal with some of the accused, offering leniency or immunity in exchange for their testimony. Or she could try to look for evidence of process crimes, such as obstruction of justice or lying to investigators, if the evidence allows. Her role here as special prosecutor is not so different from how prosecutors may reexamine cases started by their predecessors. “That is not uncommon for people in decision-making positions to have to take a look at past investigations and past decisions,” Rocah said. With so much ahead, the investigation is likely to take a while, DerOhannesian said. “Because of the quantity of information that has to be processed, the multiple legal questions that have to be answered for multiple individuals, I think it’s gonna take a lot of time,” he said. “That may be frustrating to the community, that it will be taking time to get these answers.” The office has reached out to several experienced attorneys to bolster its team, CNN reported Tuesday . The attorney general’s office, known as OAG, “has spoken with the Tompkins County District Attorney, Jane Doe’s attorney, and several candidates for outside counsel to support the investigation. The DA has agreed to cooperate, and OAG remains committed to a thorough and independent investigation guided only by the facts and the law,” a spokesperson for James said in a statement. Once the investigation is complete, James likely will either take her findings to a grand jury or issue a report explaining why she does not recommend charges. The challenges ahead for James One challenge for James is some evidence may have been lost in the two years since the October 2024 encounter. Memories may have faded, or digital evidence could have been lost or deleted. “There are real challenges looking at something several years after it happened,” Rocah said. Doe’s attorney, Thomas Giuffra, said her rape kit was conducted weeks after the incident rather than immediately afterward, potentially losing some DNA evidence. He also speculated that photos and videos of the incident may have been lost or deleted due to the failures of the original investigation. “I mean, if this was a normal investigation that was done in New York City, for example, they would have gotten search warrants,” Giuffra told CNN’s Jake Tapper on Monday. They would have grabbed every single one of these phones of these guys. They would have downloaded all this material. Another challenge for James is convincing the public to trust her independence and judgment. Late last month, she posted about Doe’s case, calling her a “survivor” and declaring, “We stand with you.” Days later, at the news conference announcing her appointment as special prosecutor, she declined to comment on the post. Andrew Miltenberg, a lawyer for one of the seven former fraternity members, on Monday called for James to recuse herself from the case, saying her statements “could reasonably be understood as accepting that the alleged conduct occurred before she assumed responsibility for determining what the evidence establishes.” Finally, any criminal charges would have to follow New York’s law defining sex crimes and lack of consent. In particular, lack of consent can result from being involuntarily “mentally incapacitated” by drugs or alcohol. But if someone voluntarily takes drugs or alcohol, they can’t be considered mentally incapacitated – an exclusion critics have called a “ loophole .” In Doe’s case, she has said she drank alcohol and took drugs that night. She also told police she was OK with an initial encounter but said she did not consent to sexual contact later in the night, according to a six-page statement obtained by CNN. Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten cited this law and Doe’s alcohol and drug use in defending his decision not to charge the accused fraternity members. However, he acknowledged he did not see all the evidence in the case before coming to that conclusion. Giuffra said Doe’s reactions to the incident were a “textbook reaction to trauma.” “Ms. Doe’s internal processing went from denial to shame and ultimately acceptance that she had been raped by people that she thought were her friends,” Giuffra told CNN Thursday. This aspect of New York law will make bringing charges a “tough climb” for prosecutors, said CNN senior legal analyst Elie Honig. Still, investigators could bring charges here under different theories, legal experts said. Even when someone consumes drugs or alcohol, they still may not be able to consent, or they could offer consent at one time and revoke it later, DerOhannesian said. It all depends on the specific facts of the case, Rocah said. “It makes a case under facts like this more challenging, but not impossible,” she said. CNN’s Kara Scannell contributed to this report. For more CNN news and newsletters create an account at CNN.com This article originally appeared on CNN at https://www.cnn.com/2026/10/11/us/cornell-allegations-investigation-whats-next

item.title: Police say mental health may be a factor in deadly Erie shooting as motive remains unclear
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Erie police are investigating mental health issues as they look for a motive in the mass killing in which a 45-year-old suspected gunman killed nine people, eight of whom were related , before killing himself at a residence on Perry Street on Oct. 9 . "I think mental health is at play here, but I think it is too soon to really go into a motive," Erie Police Chief Rick Lorah said at a news conference at City Hall on Oct. 10. He said police are looking at the mass shooting as “a domestic situation” because eight of those killed were related to one another. Lorah said the eight people who were killed were relatives and were all living at the house at 722 Perry St. He said the ninth victim was a family friend. The family friend, a 51-year-old woman, was fatally shot outside the house along with a 37-year-old sister-in-law of one of the deceased, Lorah said. Police detail sequence of killings The other people were killed inside the residence, police said. The Erie County Coroner's Office has yet to release the names of those killed , but Lorah described the people found inside as a 5-year-old boy, a 22-month-old girl, a 24-year-old woman, a 44-year-old woman, a 19-year-old man and a 21-year-old man. The 24-year-old woman was eight months pregnant, Lorah said. He said the suspected shooter, a 45-year-old man, was found dead inside the house with an apparent self-inflicted gunshot wound. Lorah said investigators believe the suspected shooter most likely killed the people inside, went outside and killed the two women, and then went back inside and killed himself. ShotSpotter alerted police to gunshots The shooting was reported to police at about 4:50 p.m. on Oct. 9. Lorah said the city's ShotSpotter gunfire-detection system alerted police to the shooting, and that patrol officers arrived at the scene within minutes and found the two women dead outside. Lorah said the ShotSpotter detected the two gunshots in the killing of the two women. No gunshots were heard once officers arrived, Lorah said. He said police determined that all nine people were killed by then. He said investigators reached the conclusion after hearing, on surveillance video, the sound of "muffled gunshots" coming from inside the house before the women were shot outside. Lorah said ShotSpotter "rarely if ever can pick up gunshots inside homes." The officers who first arrived at the scene "were met with an eerie silence," Lorah said. "No movement. No audible sounds coming from inside the residence. No gunshots. No screams." Police used drones "to assess conditions within the residence" before SWAT officers broke down multiple doors and entered the house and found those killed inside, according to the city. Family, community mourns: Aunt of 22-month-old victim speaks about Erie shootings at vigil 2 women shot outside arrived at house in distress, police say Lorah said investigators are looking into what led the two women killed outside to arrive at the residence. The other woman was a sister-in-law of one of those killed, and Lorah said she and the family friend got to the house in a state of distress, based on surveillance video and interviews with neighbors. He said the two women pounded on the front door and sought help from neighbors. The suspected shooter came out of the house and called to them, Lorah said. He said the women ran toward the shooter and he killed them. Lorah also said the women and the shooter spoke to one another before he shot them. "They must have known that something was going on," Lorah said. "They didn't contact us, so we don't know what that is yet." He said police would try to gather evidence from the women's cellphones and other sources. 'What happened was horrific' The suspected shooter was found with a .40-caliber handgun on him, Lorah said. He said the gun was registered to the man, and that police believe he was legally allowed to possess it. Lorah said the suspected shooter last had an interaction with the police in 2022, but did not have further information immediately available. Lorah spoke at the news conference along with Mayor Daria Devlin and Erie County District Attorney Elizabeth Hirz, who said her office is working with the police in its investigation. Hirz, Lorah and Devlin expressed condolences to the families of those killed. They said the shooting is unlike anything the city has ever seen. "I want to start by speaking directly to the families who lost loved ones last night. I am so deeply sorry," Devlin said. "What happened was horrific, and I know there is nothing I can say today that will make this any easier. But I want you to know that our entire community is thinking of you, grieving with you, and here to support you." Contact Ed Palattella at epalattella@usatodayco.com or 814-870-1813. item.title: Mystery at Russian plague lab as WHO struggles to explain young worker's death
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
GENEVA (AP) — The World Health Organization said Saturday it still doesn’t know what caused the death of a young worker at a lab in Russia that focuses on plague and other illnesses. The U.N. health agency has cited initial, unconfirmed reports suggesting pneumonic plague, a severe disease less common than the better-known bubonic plague linked to the Black Death in the Middle Ages. Pneumonic plague spreads from person to person, causing a severe form of pneumonia, but recovery rates are high if it is detected and treated in time. WHO, in its first full Disease Outbreak News since the case emerged earlier this month, called for a continued investigation. Russian health officials, it said, had conducted more than 5,500 tests and found no evidence of any dangerous pathogenic microorganisms. “Additional clinical, epidemiological and laboratory information, including confirmation of the diagnosis in the deceased laboratory worker, is required to improve confidence in the assessment,” WHO said. WHO continued to refer to “a purported second case” that, in emailed explanations to The Associated Press, it previously attributed to two tabloid news outlets in Britain and Serbia that cited unspecified reports in Russia. Russia has denied any such second case. This article originally appeared on Associated Press at https://www.yahoo.com/news/world/articles/mystery-surrounds-young-workers-death-201307325.html

item.title: Ozempic or retirement? Some users are sacrificing savings to pay for prescriptions.
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
( NewsNation ) — Americans taking popular GLP-1 medications such as Ozempic, Wegovy and Zepbound may be facing a new financial dilemma: save for retirement or pay for the drugs helping improve their health. A new survey from the Nationwide Retirement Institute found that 51% of current GLP-1 users worry they may have to choose between medication costs and retirement savings. The survey suggests those concerns are already affecting financial decisions. According to Nationwide, 54% of current users have changed their financial behavior to afford the medications, including 17% who have taken on debt, 14% who have withdrawn money from savings or retirement accounts and 14% who have reduced retirement contributions. Counterfeit Ozempic scheme traced to China, feds say Out-of-pocket costs remain a major challenge, especially for patients whose insurance does not fully cover treatment. According to InvestmentNews , users without full coverage spend an average of $203 a month out of pocket, even as many expect to remain on the drugs long term to maintain weight-loss and metabolic benefits. Yet many users believe the health benefits may outweigh the financial sacrifice. The Nationwide survey found that 88% of current GLP-1 users are more optimistic about their long-term health, while 64% say they may retire later because they feel healthier. Nearly six in 10 respondents said improved health makes them feel less pressure to increase retirement savings. GLP-1 drugs linked to nutritional deficiencies in kids, study says Financial planners are increasingly grappling with questions that barely existed a few years ago, including whether clients should reduce retirement contributions to afford GLP-1 medications and whether improved health today could offset future healthcare costs. Kristi Martin Rodriguez of the Nationwide Retirement Institute said rising GLP-1 use is creating new financial planning challenges. "If what you're spending on your health today is competing with what you're saving for tomorrow, that needs to be part of the financial planning conversation," Rodriguez said. The findings underscore a broader affordability challenge as demand for GLP-1 drugs continues to soar. While insurers and some employers have expanded coverage for obesity and diabetes treatments, many Americans still face substantial out-of-pocket expenses. According to Nationwide, 59% of current users worry about being able to afford GLP-1 medications in retirement, raising the prospect that these drugs could become a major retirement-planning issue in the years ahead. item.title: Bracing for the midterms, Trump says he will be blamed if Republicans lose
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Midterm elections often punish the sitting president’s party, and Trump’s popularity isn’t helping the GOP’s cause. (Mandel Ngan / AFP via Getty) CLARKSVILLE, Tenn. — Even as he makes a case that Republicans should win the midterm congressional elections, President Donald Trump is bracing for the fallout should they lose. Someone is bound to get blamed, and Trump said at a rally in Tennessee on Saturday that he expects it will be him. “If we don’t win the midterms, they’re going to blame me,” Trump said. “You know that. And if we do win them, I will get no credit whatsoever. It’s true. I won’t get any.” “But I’m working my ass off,” he added. “You better get out there and vote.” Trump is in “grind it out mode” ahead of the midterms, a person familiar with the matter said, and is prepared for the worst-case election outcome. Midterm elections often punish the sitting president’s party, and Trump’s popularity isn’t helping the GOP’s cause. Only 38% approve of his performance in office, compared with 59% who disapprove, according to an NBC News average of polls. Trump is looking to defy historical trends by motivating core supporters who might be inclined to sit out the elections, and by offering voters an unusual sweetener if they preserve the Republican majority in the House and Senate. He closed his hour-and-a-half-long speech with a reminder that “with your vote on Nov. 3, you’ll get $5,000.” That’s the size of the payment he’s promising to send adults if Republicans win the midterms. The total price tag is estimated at $1.3 trillion. Trump is indeed pushing himself as the elections approach, keeping up a frenetic schedule. Tennessee was the seventh state he has visited since the start of October. He had planned to fly to an eighth, Alabama, later in the day to attend the Georgia-Alabama football game, but canceled the trip with Hurricane Isaias bearing down. Trump used part of the rally to debunk the idea that his popularity has dropped. In a social media post Saturday, he wrote that the notion that he’s in disfavor is a “false narrative.” Onstage, he played a CNN clip showing that his support among his MAGA supporters is nearly unanimous and has shown no slippage since the 2024 elections. (CNN was one of three news outlets that the Trump administration last month banned from White House grounds.) “I’m very popular, I really am,” Trump told the crowd. For Trump, traveling to a deep-red congressional district in a deep-red state like Tennessee might seem like time wasted in the few weeks left before the midterms. Republicans are expected to sweep the state’s House and Senate races. Trump’s rally took place in an indoor arena in a northern Tennessee county that he won by 18 percentage points in the 2024 presidential race. Trump himself suggested the state’s congressional candidates are already on a glide path to victory, with or without him. “These guys are all going to win,” he said. “These congressmen are phenomenal. So, I’m saying, ‘What the hell am I doing in Tennessee?’” Answering his own question, he said he wanted to “reward the places that have automatically treated you well.” Trump won Tennessee in all three of his presidential campaigns. Other Republicans said Trump is hewing to a sensible strategy: mobilizing his supporters and making sure they vote on Nov. 3 even though he’s not on the ballot. “It rallies the base,” Rep. Tim Burchett, R-Tenn., said in an interview before Trump took the stage. “And that’s really what we’ve got to see in a midterm election. That’s what you’ve got to have: the base.” Much of Trump’s address was a recitation of what he considers his chief accomplishments. He cited a rise in the median household income in his first year in office and a drop in the nation’s poverty rate. Never shy about rebranding American landmarks, he also mused about renaming the Atlantic or Pacific oceans in ways that would ensure he’s not forgotten. Presumably in jest, he said, “We call it, ‘Trump Ocean.’ Or, ‘Ocean of the Americas,’ something like that. No, we have to. We should have before I get out, I think we should have an ocean and we need a great river.” This article was originally published on NBCNews.com This article originally appeared on NBC News at https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/donald-trump/bracing-midterms-trump-says-will-blamed-republicans-lose-rcna602512

item.title: Pope Leo to undergo surgery after doctors discover growth on his lung
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
By Joshua McElwee VATICAN CITY, Oct 11 (Reuters) - Pope Leo said on Sunday that doctors had detected a small growth on his lung during a recent health check and he would be undergoing surgery ‌this week to remove it, in the first health scare of the 71-year-old pontiff's tenure. Leo told pilgrims in ‌St. Peter's Square for his weekly Sunday prayer that the growth, a small nodule, was "well-contained" and had been spotted early. The Vatican did not say ​whether the nodule is believed to be malignant. "Recently, during some medical examinations, doctors found a localized nodule in my lung," said the pontiff. "It was detected at a very early stage and is well contained." "The doctors believe it is advisable to intervene, so, following their advice, I have decided to undergo surgery to remove it," he said. "The operation is already scheduled for the ‌next few days." A nodule on the lung ⁠is a small, localised lesion that can be benign. The American Thoracic Society says fewer than 5% of lung nodules overall prove cancerous, although risk rises with age, size, and other ⁠factors such as smoking. "Lung nodules are fairly common and are often benign," said Stephen Liu, a lung cancer expert at Georgetown University in Washington and division chief of hematology-oncology at MedStar Georgetown University Hospital. "When there is sufficient concern, and when it is safe ​to do ​so, based on the location of the nodule and the ​overall health of the patient, surgical removal can ‌provide a definitive diagnosis," he said. LEO A RELATIVELY YOUNG POPE, PLAYS SPORTS Leo, elected pope by the world's cardinals in May 2025, is relatively young for a Church leader. He enjoys sports, including tennis, and is not known to be a smoker or to previously have had health issues. Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni wished the pope well. "I would like to express to the Holy Father my personal support, and that of the Italian government, as he faces this challenge in the ‌coming days," she said in a statement. "The serenity and composure with ​which he spoke about it (today) ...are reassuring," Meloni added. The late Pope Francis, Leo's ​predecessor, died at age 88. He was hospitalised several ​times as he grew frail in his later years. He did not usually announce his ‌hospital visits in advance, sometimes sparking a media ​frenzy over his health. The Vatican press ​office said Leo's recovery from surgery was expected to take about a week. It did not immediately provide further details about the pope's health. Leo keeps a busy schedule and is due to make an 11-day tour ​of Uruguay, Argentina and Peru from ‌November 6-17. Before mentioning his health issue in his address on Sunday, the pope referred to the trip, ​thanking Catholics for their prayers "for the pastoral visit I will undertake." (Reporting by Joshua McElwee, Francesca Landini and ​Gavin JonesEditing by Tomasz Janowski, Alexandra Hudson and Susan Fenton) This article originally appeared on Reuters at https://www.yahoo.com/news/us/articles/pope-leo-says-undergo-surgery-104303066.html
